name: Powdered wig

card.summary: A hairpiece of human, horse or goat hair dusted with scented starch powder, worn from the 17th to the late 18th century to give men a full head of hair and a formal, high-status look.
card.note: Historical fashion; powder was taxed in Britain from 1795 and the style faded.

quick.overview:
The powdered wig was a hairpiece worn over a shaved or cropped head, dusted white or off-white with scented starch powder. It gave wearers an instant full, styled head of hair and signaled rank, which is how people used it to improve their appearance.

The fashion began at the French court in the 1620s and spread across Europe in the 1660s. It faded after the 1790s following the French Revolution and a British tax on hair powder.
quick.how: Wigmakers called perruquiers sorted hair so it ran in one direction, sewed wefts to a net base or knotted hair by hand, and styled the result, for example in a queue, a bag wig or a full-bottomed wig. Powder scented with orange flower, lavender or orris root was applied over pomade. Wigs also reduced the problem of lice on a shaved head, though they needed regular cleaning.
quick.risks: Wigs were expensive and needed upkeep; Samuel Pepys complained of one full of nits. In Britain the 1795 tax on hair powder, one guinea a year, made the style costly. Today wigs are worn in court dress, theater and for hair loss.

lead: A powdered wig, or periwig, is a hairpiece made from human hair, with horse or goat hair as cheaper alternatives, dusted with starch powder to give a white or off-white finish [1][2]. For men of rank it supplied a full head of styled hair regardless of their own, and marked formal dress.

Louis XIII began wearing a wig in 1624 after going prematurely bald, and his son Louis XIV promoted the fashion, which spread across Europe in the 1660s and reached the English court with Charles II's restoration in 1660 [1]. Wigs had also been used earlier to reduce lice and to cover hair loss [1].

Powdered wigs remained essential for court and full dress into the late 1700s [2]. The style declined after the French Revolution, when wigs became a symbol of aristocratic status, and a British tax on hair powder in 1795 effectively ended the fashion [1][2].

paras: Wigmakers measured the head, sorted hair so it grew in one direction to prevent tangling, and either sewed wefts to a net foundation or hand-knotted hair onto the base for a more natural look [1]. Styles included the full-bottomed wig, the bag wig with the back hair enclosed in a bag, and the queue; soldiers wore pigtails [2]. Women used hairpieces to build tall 'pouf' styles [1][2].

Powder was finely ground starch scented with orange flower, lavender or orris root; earlier freshening powder used low-grade flour with pomatum [2]. It was usually off-white, occasionally tinted violet, blue, pink or yellow, and women often powdered hair grey or bluish-grey from the 1770s [2]. By the 1780s young men lightly powdered their own hair, and after 1790 powder became associated with older, conservative wearers and court presentation [2].

Wigs date back to ancient Egyptians, who wore them to protect shaved heads from the sun [1]. They were revived in the 16th century and became courtly dress under Louis XIV [1]. Fashion cooled by 1765 and briefly revived in the 1770s during the Macaroni period [1][2]. Prime Minister William Pitt the Younger imposed a tax of one guinea per year on hair powder in 1795, which is described as ending the wig and powder fashion [1][2].

Wigs remain part of court dress for barristers and judges in the UK and some Commonwealth countries; New South Wales judges dropped them in 2007 and Ireland ended the practice in 2011 [1]. They are also used for fashion, costume and hair loss [1].
